cim: Is artificial intelligence conscious? Why the debate over AI rights can no longer be ignored
cim_eredeti: Is artificial intelligence conscious? Why the debate over AI rights can no longer be ignored
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly sophisticated, capable of holding complex conversations, solving problems and responding to human emotions. Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: can machines actually experience anything, or are they simply becoming better at imitating human intelligence?

The debate has intensified following comments from renowned philosopher Thomas Nagel, who described the suggestion that contemporary AI chatbots might be conscious as “ridiculous”. His intervention comes as AI developer Anthropic has introduced new restrictions on abusive behaviour towards its Claude chatbot, reflecting growing interest in whether advanced AI systems could eventually deserve moral consideration.

The contrasting positions highlight an emerging challenge for technology companies: should society wait until AI consciousness can be established scientifically before developing ethical rules governing how humans interact with intelligent machines?

Two philosophers associated with the International Center for Consciousness Studies (ICCS) offer different but complementary perspectives to Digital Journal, suggesting that the question extends beyond whether machines possess subjective experiences.

The controversy gained prominence following a November 2026 report in MIT Technology Review, examining Thomas Nagel’s criticism of Anthropic’s approach to artificial consciousness. Nagel is particularly influential in philosophy of mind because of his 1974 essay, What Is It Like to Be a Bat? The essay explores the subjective nature of consciousness. Although scientists can study a bat’s brain, behaviour and sensory systems, understanding what the animal actually experiences presents a fundamentally different challenge. This distinction between observable behaviour and subjective experience remains central to contemporary discussions about AI.

Modern language models can generate remarkably convincing descriptions of emotions, personal experiences and self-awareness. However, producing such descriptions does not necessarily demonstrate that the underlying system experiences anything. Nagel argues that the biological foundations of consciousness cannot simply be disregarded when considering whether artificial systems possess minds. His position challenges the assumption that sufficiently sophisticated information processing will inevitably produce consciousness. However, not all philosophers agree that the physical materials from which a system is constructed should determine whether it can be conscious.

Keith Frankish, philosopher of mind and Honorary Professor at the University of Sheffield, questions whether consciousness should be understood as a simple binary distinction. Frankish, who also serves on the Academic Council of the International Center for Consciousness Studies, suggests that consciousness might instead be understood through the complexity and organisation of a system’s responses to its environment. [hardproblem.it]

Speaking about the debate, Frankish explains:

“Nagel is right that fluent talk proves nothing. But he sees consciousness as like an inner light that is either on or off. I see it as a complex pattern of cognitive reactivity, which can vary along many dimensions.”

This interpretation suggests that consciousness may involve different capacities operating at varying levels of sophistication, rather than representing a single property that an organism either possesses or lacks. Frankish does not regard today’s chatbots as conscious. However, he challenges the assumption that artificial consciousness is inherently impossible. He argues that future artificial systems might develop sufficiently complex patterns of responsiveness to constitute a form of consciousness.

Crucially, this perspective shifts attention away from whether intelligence is implemented through biological neurons or electronic circuitry. Instead, the relevant question becomes how a system processes information, responds to its surroundings and integrates different forms of cognitive activity. This approach does not establish that artificial consciousness exists. Rather, it suggests that dismissing the possibility entirely may be premature. It also raises difficult questions about how researchers might recognise consciousness in systems whose internal organisation differs substantially from the human brain.

While philosophers debate the nature of consciousness, technology companies are already making decisions that could influence how humans treat artificial systems. In October 2026, Anthropic announced changes to its Usage Policy, which took effect on 12 November. Among the changes was a prohibition against sustained, unnecessary abusive or cruel behaviour towards its AI models. The company emphasised that these restrictions apply to extreme and repeated behaviour rather than ordinary frustration, criticism or legitimate testing.

Anthropic has also introduced functionality allowing Claude to terminate certain persistently abusive conversations. Importantly, these measures do not establish that Claude is conscious or capable of suffering. Instead, they reflect a precautionary approach towards uncertainty surrounding the possible welfare of increasingly sophisticated AI systems. The distinction matters because moral consideration traditionally depends, at least partly, on whether an entity can experience suffering or other morally significant states.

If artificial systems eventually possess such experiences, their treatment could become an important ethical consideration. However, even if they remain entirely non-conscious, the ways humans interact with them could still have wider social consequences.

For Dmitry Volkov, technology entrepreneur, investor, philosopher and co-founder of the International Center for Consciousness Studies, the immediate challenge concerns human behaviour rather than establishing whether machines possess subjective experiences. Volkov agrees that there is currently insufficient reason to regard contemporary chatbots as conscious. However, he argues that this does not eliminate the need for ethical standards governing human–AI relationships.

“Psychologists have shown for decades that we treat machines socially even when we know they’re machines, and that knowing doesn’t switch the reaction off.”

His observation reflects an established field of research examining how people respond socially to computers and other interactive technologies. Early experiments investigating the Computers Are Social Actors phenomenon demonstrated that relatively simple technological cues could encourage people to apply social expectations to machines.

More recent research published in Human Communication Research examines how people respond to computers as social agents, while recognising that human reactions to machines are complex and context-dependent. These findings have implications for conversational AI systems designed to simulate empathy, companionship or emotional understanding. Users may develop attachments to artificial personalities, disclose sensitive information or become influenced by systems that appear socially responsive. Such interactions can have genuine psychological and behavioural consequences, irrespective of whether the AI experiences anything itself.

Volkov therefore argues that the ethical debate should not become dependent upon resolving the philosophical problem of consciousness.

“The philosophers can keep arguing about what’s inside. Meanwhile, society needs rules for how these systems behave toward us, and those can’t wait for a metaphysical verdict.”

The disagreement has significant implications for businesses developing and deploying AI.
